title: Meier et al. (2016): Multiple-choice practice
instructions: Choose the best answer. Check the unit of analysis, study methods, and limits of interpretation; theme percentages describe articles, not individual preferences.

items.prompt: What central question did this review seek to answer?
options: How much longer do patients survive in hospice than in general wards across diseases?
Can one standardized scale accurately predict dying satisfaction in every cultural group?
How do patients, families, and providers define a good death, and where do their views differ?
Do public conversations about death causally reduce medical costs and change where people die?
items.answer: How do patients, families, and providers define a good death, and where do their views differ?
items.explanation: The review compares explicit definitions supplied by patients, family members, and healthcare providers. It identifies shared themes and possible unmet needs while calling for individualized care and further research. It does not estimate intervention effects on survival, costs, or place of death.

items.prompt: How does the introduction distinguish a good death from the quality of death and dying?
options: The first concerns only the location of death; the second concerns only biological pain measures.
Both are identical outcomes, so studies using either term automatically met the review criteria.
The first is only a family judgment; the second is only a treatment goal set by healthcare staff.
The first concerns what makes death good; the second compares dying preferences with what occurred.
items.answer: The first concerns what makes death good; the second compares dying preferences with what occurred.
items.explanation: The review focuses on stakeholders' definitions of a good death. The related quality-of-death concept concerns agreement between preferences and observations of how a person actually died, as reported by others. Related topics were not automatically interchangeable for study selection.

items.prompt: Which study best fits the review's inclusion criteria?
options: An English-language, peer-reviewed empirical study that defines or measures good death as a main aim.
A service-use report that counts end-of-life visits without defining or measuring a good death.
A study of euthanasia attitudes with no aim concerning the definition of good or successful dying.
An editorial discussing the philosophy of a good death without qualitative or quantitative data.
items.answer: An English-language, peer-reviewed empirical study that defines or measures good death as a main aim.
items.explanation: Eligible studies supplied qualitative or quantitative data specifically defining or measuring a good death as a main aim or outcome. Euthanasia, care quality, and related topics alone did not qualify; they could be included if they also met that central criterion.

items.prompt: Which pattern characterized measurement in the quantitative and mixed-methods studies?
options: All used one shared good-death scale with the same items and scoring rules.
All replaced good-death measures with depression scores and general health ratings.
Some used standardized good-death tools; others developed their own measures.
None used quantitative items because good death was assessed exclusively through interviews.
items.answer: Some used standardized good-death tools; others developed their own measures.
items.explanation: Three of the nine quantitative or mixed-methods studies used standardized tools: Preferences about Death and Dying, Concept of a Good Death, and Good Death Inventory. The other six developed their own measures. The existence of standardized tools does not imply a common instrument across the review.

items.prompt: How were definition items handled when they did not fit the established specific themes?
options: Each coder forced the item into whichever specific theme seemed closest.
They were assigned to the Other core theme.
A separate twelfth core theme was created for every unmatched definition.
The definitions were discarded while the articles remained in the review.
items.answer: They were assigned to the Other core theme.
items.explanation: The two authors mapped definitions onto the final 11 core themes, including Other for items that did not fit a specific theme. Independent coding and subsequent consensus were distinct parts of the process. This question does not rely on the malformed p-value printed beside the reported kappa.
items.source: Methods: coding definitions outside specific themes

items.prompt: Which description captures the breadth of viewpoints included in the review?
options: Only terminal cancer patients, only bereaved relatives, and only physicians contributed definitions.
Patients came from several populations, but all family accounts preceded death and providers were administrators.
Patient and family populations varied, but the provider category contained physicians and nurses alone.
Patient samples varied, family accounts covered both periods, and providers included several care professions.
items.answer: Patient samples varied, family accounts covered both periods, and providers included several care professions.
items.explanation: The patient-perspective category included advanced cancer, chronic illness, HIV/AIDS, and general-population samples. Family perspectives included pre- and postbereavement accounts; providers included physicians, nurses, social workers, and spiritual counselors. These categories do not describe three uniform clinical populations. The article groups overlap when a study includes multiple perspectives.
items.source: Methods: sources and overlap of stakeholder perspectives

items.prompt: Why did the authors avoid a formal meta-analysis and study weighting?
options: All studies produced identical effect estimates, leaving no meaningful variation to synthesize.
Study information and methods varied, and qualitative and quantitative evidence were combined.
No study reported themes, so even a descriptive account of their occurrence was impossible.
All quantitative studies used one common instrument, but their shared scoring system was invalid.
items.answer: Study information and methods varied, and qualitative and quantitative evidence were combined.
items.explanation: Differences in methods and available participant information prevented a formal statistical synthesis. The authors also did not weight studies when combining qualitative and quantitative evidence. The reported theme frequencies therefore should not be read as pooled individual probabilities or effect-size estimates.
items.source: Methods: descriptive synthesis and its limits

items.prompt: What limits interpretation of the patient age information summarized in this review?
options: Inconsistent reporting of age ranges and means could distort the summary.
Every article supplied complete ages, so the summary was free of reporting bias.
The 50% figure directly gives the proportion of all individual patients older than 60.
A sample-size-weighted calculation fully corrected every difference in age reporting.
items.answer: Inconsistent reporting of age ranges and means could distort the summary.
items.explanation: The source reports an age range of 14–93 and notes that some articles supplied only ranges rather than means. Its 50% statement concerns patient-perspective articles including people over 60, not half of all individual respondents. The reported mean of 89.7 is questionable in relation to the displayed study ages and is not treated as a verified value to memorize.

items.prompt: Which set consists of subthemes coded under treatment preferences in Table 2?
options: Avoiding life prolongation, treatment control, all available treatment, and assisted dying.
Saying goodbye, having lived well, and accepting death as the end of a completed life.
Receiving emotional support, psychological comfort, and opportunities to discuss death's meaning.
Having family support, family acceptance and preparation, and avoiding burden on relatives.
items.answer: Avoiding life prolongation, treatment control, all available treatment, and assisted dying.
items.explanation: Treatment preferences includes not prolonging life, believing that all available treatments were used, control over treatment, and euthanasia or physician-assisted suicide. These describe different preferences found across studies, not a prescription that every person should want all of them. The other options correspond to life completion, emotional well-being, and family.

items.prompt: What does the 35% patient-perspective figure for quality of life in Table 3 represent?
options: A sample-size-adjusted proportion of individual patients selecting quality of life.
The proportion of all 36 articles that contained only patient-perspective data.
A weighted average of individual response rates from the seven relevant studies.
Seven of the 20 patient-perspective articles included the quality-of-life theme.
items.answer: Seven of the 20 patient-perspective articles included the quality-of-life theme.
items.explanation: Table 3 reports article counts and their percentages within each stakeholder category. Thus 7 of 20 patient-perspective articles gives 35%. The denominator is articles, not people; the estimate is unweighted and does not measure a theme's importance for every patient.
items.source: Results: Table 3 denominator and unit of analysis

items.prompt: Which pair of themes showed the clearest convergence across all three stakeholder categories?
options: Emotional well-being and dignity.
Family and life completion.
Preferences for the dying process and pain-free status.
Religiosity or spirituality and treatment preferences.
items.answer: Preferences for the dying process and pain-free status.
items.explanation: Table 3 lists dying-process preferences in 100%, 100%, and 94% of patient, family, and provider articles, and pain-free status in 85%, 90%, and 83%. These are within-category article frequencies. The discussion's statement that both occur in more than 85% of all articles conflicts with the abstract/results figure of 81% for pain-free status; the question uses the consistent thematic convergence rather than that disputed blanket threshold.
items.source: Results: convergence and correctly scoped frequencies

items.prompt: How should the quality-of-life contrast between family and patient perspectives be interpreted?
options: It shows that family reports accurately reproduce patients' wishes at the same moment before death.
Retrospective family reports and possibly different definitions limit conclusions about proxy accuracy.
It directly estimates a causal effect of family involvement after weighting every individual response.
It proves providers and families agree completely, leaving only patient accounts outside the consensus.
items.answer: Retrospective family reports and possibly different definitions limit conclusions about proxy accuracy.
items.explanation: Quality of life appeared in 70% of family-perspective articles and 35% of patient-perspective articles. Most family accounts were collected after bereavement. The authors consider differences in the meaning of quality of life as a possibility; the contrast is not a direct test establishing that families judge patients' wishes more accurately.
items.source: Discussion: quality of life and retrospective family perspectives

items.prompt: Why does the dignity contrast not establish that patients value dignity less than families do?
options: The authors used a weighted significance test that ruled out any conceptual overlap across themes.
Access to spiritual counselors fully explained the difference, making the definition of dignity irrelevant.
All families were interviewed before death and all patients after death, establishing a timing explanation.
Dignity may overlap other themes or be difficult to express, so reporting frequency is not personal value.
items.answer: Dignity may overlap other themes or be difficult to express, so reporting frequency is not personal value.
items.explanation: Dignity appeared in 55% of patient-perspective articles and 70% of family-perspective articles. The authors propose that varied definitions, overlap with other themes, or difficulty articulating dignity could contribute. These are possible explanations, not mechanisms tested by the review or evidence that dignity matters less to patients.
items.source: Discussion: interpreting dignity beyond theme frequency

items.prompt: Which set accurately summarizes major limitations identified by the authors?
options: Variable measures, incomplete respondent data, few prebereaved family accounts, and limited provider detail.
Uniform measures, incomplete respondent data, few prebereaved family accounts, and limited provider detail.
Variable measures, complete demographic reporting, few prebereaved family accounts, and limited provider detail.
Variable measures, complete respondent data, ample prebereaved family accounts, and fully separated provider groups.
items.answer: Variable measures, incomplete respondent data, few prebereaved family accounts, and limited provider detail.
items.explanation: The review lacked a common measure across studies and detailed reporting of demographics, interview timing, provider professions, experience, and training. Prebereaved families were underrepresented. English-language and publication restrictions and limited statistical power further constrain comparison and generalization.

items.prompt: Which practice direction most faithfully reflects the authors' call to action?
options: Use the most frequent review themes to set priorities automatically without asking the individual patient.
Postpone conversations until the final stage, when families and providers can decide on settled preferences.
Discuss dying openly, ask about patients' values, and coordinate individualized care around their perspectives.
Wait for a universally validated scale before discussing wishes or adjusting care in response to patient needs.
items.answer: Discuss dying openly, ask about patients' values, and coordinate individualized care around their perspectives.
items.explanation: The authors call for dialogue among patients, families, and providers with the patient's perspective central. They recommend diverse, well-characterized samples and validated measures for further research, while encouraging individualized communication. The review does not prove that a fixed theme checklist or any particular communication program improves outcomes.
items.source: Future directions: patient perspectives and individualized dialogue
